headlines.title: Oakland restaurant to raise funds for victims of Colombia earthquake
headlines.description: A popular East Bay restaurant is stepping up to help those impacted by the devastating earthquake that hit Colombia. For the owners, the disaster hits especially close to home. On Aug. 17, popular Colombian restaurant Parche in Oakland will be raising money for earthquake relief. The restaurant will match all empanada and cocktail sales from 5 p.m. until closing, and the money is going toward local relief efforts in Colombia. The co-owner of Parche, Paul Iglesias, was visiting one of the impacted areas just weeks ago on a culinary trip. “It was heartbreaking to here that the actual house I was staying in for a week basically crumbled to the ground,” Iglesias said. His parents grew up in Colombia, and Iglesias says he’s now watching communities he knows sort through the damage left behind by that devastating 7.4 magnitude earthquake. Colombia Aug 11 Earthquakes Aug 11 Earthquakes Aug 10 The search for survivors is becoming more desperate by the day, after the quake struck western Colombia Monday, killing hundreds and injuring thousands. A rescue crew member saying crews have not slept as they search through the rubble of thousands of destroyed homes. Still, there were signs of hope. A video showed a woman being pulled to safety from beneath thick concrete. Crews also rescued a 6-month-old baby found alive, but the clock is ticking, search teams are stretched thin, and so are medical teams. Dozens of hospitals and health clinics were damaged in the quake, leaving doctors and nurses scrambling to help those who survived. Now, the popular East Bay restaurant is now doing its part to help those in need back in Colombia. “The thing that we said was oh my gosh we have to do something, what are we going to do? We are in Oakland, California, but we can have an event to celebrate our culture and our community,” Iglesias said. For Iglesias, helping the country his family calls home was both an easy and necessary decision. “It’s because we can we should, right? I don’t know any other way and it’s my culture, it’s my parents, it’s my heritage, it’s just an extension and it’s something that’s super important,” Iglesias said.

headlines.title: Crews knock down 1-alarm fire at Burger King in West San Jose
headlines.description: Crews knocked down a one-alarm fire reported early Thursday morning at a Burger King restaurant in West San Jose, according to fire officials. Firefighters were alerted around 5:15 a.m. to the blaze at the Burger King restaurant in the 5100 block of Moorpark Avenue. The flames were knocked down around 6:30 a.m, the San Jose Fire Department said on social media. The department did not immediately disclose the cause of the fire.

headlines.title: Northbound I-680 in Dublin reopens after police activity
headlines.description: All lanes of northbound Interstate 680 at Interstate 580 in Dublin reopened Thursday morning following police activity, according to the California Highway Patrol. CHP had issued a Sig Alert for the area, with all northbound I-680 traffic being diverted onto eastbound I-580. All lanes reopened as of 7:06 a.m., CHP said. headlines.title: Firefighters battle wildfire west of Lake Tahoe
headlines.description: A wildfire popped up west of Lake Tahoe Wednesday, according to Cal Fire. Crews are battling the Talbot Fire, that’s now grown to 200 acres and it’s creating huge plumes of smoke. It started around 5 p.m. near the French Meadows Reservoir, south of I-80, and west of the Lake in a remote area. Although this is in a remote area, an evacuation warning is in effect for “Talbot Fire Zone 1,” according to Cal Fire. The fire has not been contained.

headlines.title: Foster City condo complex fire victims ask officials to declare state of emergency
headlines.description: The victims of the fire at a condominium complex in Foster City are asking elected officials to push for a state of emergency declaration. The fire affected about 50 units, left roughly 150 people displaced and injured four firefighters. “I had postcards from my grandmother, for example, who passed away when I was a child,” Kelly said. “My husband had the letters I sent him when he deployed to Iraq.” “Over 100 of us, overnight, became homeless essentially. It is a disaster and in our opinion a state of emergency and we really hope to get that support from our local and state representatives, as well,” Kelly continued. A group of condo owners and residents have now sent a letter to their local elected officials including Foster City’s mayor and their San Mateo County supervisor, urging them to push the state to declare a state of emergency. “It would not magically give us as owners and residents our property back or replace anything for us, but it would give us stronger insurance protections, stronger resources to help rebuild,” Kelly said. In certain instances, the governor can authorize the state department of emergency services to provide financial relief for emergency actions, restoration of public facilities and infrastructure and hazard mitigation. “Everyone’s lost their belongings, people are still searching for their pets,” condominium owner Meenakshi said. San Mateo County Supervisor Noelia Corzo in a statement said residents deserve the support and resources they need to recover, but that the county defers to Foster City whether a state of emergency should be declared. She adds that they continue to stand ready to deploy county departments to support unmet needs. “A lot of people are vulnerable, and we need that support from the govt, we have done our best, and now we need the govt and the local authorities to stand up for us,” Meenakshi said. NBC Bay Area reached out to Foster City’s mayor and Governor Gavin Newsom’s Office, but hasn’t heard back.

headlines.title: Woman struck, killed while riding electric scooter in San Francisco identified
headlines.description: A woman who was struck and killed Friday while riding an electric scooter on Market Street was identified by the San Francisco Medical Examiner’s Office. Yebin Kim, a 32-year-old woman from San Francisco, was identified as the victim of the collision. On Friday at 8:18 a.m., San Francisco police responded to reports of a vehicle collision at Powell and Market streets. At the scene, officers found Kim in the street and provided first aid until medical personnel arrived. She was pronounced dead on scene. Police said the collision was between a standup electric scooter and a commercial vehicle. The driver of the vehicle was located and cooperated with the investigation. The SFPD Traffic Collision Investigation Unit is conducting the investigation. Anyone with information is asked to contact SFPD at 415-575-4444 or text a tip to TIP411.

headlines.title: ‘Their daughters were their world': Aunt speaks after $33M Redwood City crash verdict
headlines.description: On Tuesday, a San Mateo County jury awarded $33 million to twin girls who lost both of their parents in a high-speed street-racing crash in Redwood City nearly four years ago. The girls’ maternal aunt, Liza Spiridon, who adopted the now 11-year-old girls after the deadly crash, tells NBC Bay Area they finally feel some measure of justice, but said justice is not only responsibility but also remorse, reform, and making sure the next family doesn’t go through what they’ve been and will continue to go through. The verdict followed a roughly three-week wrongful death trial over the crash that killed Greg Ammen, 44, and Grace Spiridon, 42, as the family was heading home to San Carlos with their then-7-year-old twin daughters. The jury awarded the girls $33 million in economic and non-economic damages and found both other drivers involved, Cesar Morales and Kyle Harrison, along with Morales’ parents, Arnold Morales and Susana Salto Alvarez, liable. Redwood City Aug 11 Redwood City Jul 16 Redwood City Jan 17, 2025 Jurors assigned 60% of the fault to Cesar Morales, 20% to Arnold Morales, 15% to Kyle Harrison and 5% to Susana Salto Alvarez. “When the truth prevails, it doesn’t just vindicate — it heals,” Spiridon said following the verdict. “It gives grief somewhere to rest, turns silence into evidence, and hands the people left behind something they can finally stand on: not closure, but clarity.” Greg worked as an audio engineer at Dolby and Grace served as Head of New Service Introduction at Google. Family members and colleagues described them during the civil trial as successful and dedicated parents whose lives centered around their daughters. “Their daughters were their world. There’s nothing they would not do for them…they were involved in their classrooms volunteering, going to every single soccer game,” Liza Spiridon told NBC Bay Area. “Grace teaching the girls how to bake, Greg showing the girls woodworking, his Boy Scout side growing up.” Prosecutors determined Cesar Morales, then 17, and Harrison, then 23, were engaged in an illegal street race moments before the crash. Morales’ vehicle struck the Ammen family’s car as it was turning left. Harrison slowed down but did not stop after witnessing the crash. During the civil trial, witnesses described pulling the girls from the mangled vehicle. Spiridon said the twins have undergone intensive trauma therapy following the deaths of their parents. “They did more so early on” Spiridon said when asked whether the girls talk about the crash or their parents. “Now it comes up occasionally or when there’s a song or something that reminds them of mommy and daddy.” During the civil trial Jurors heard evidence that Morales was driving approximately 105 to 110 mph before the collision. The defense tried arguing Grace Spiridon was partially responsible for the crash because she turned left in front of the speeding cars, but the jurors ultimately disagreed. The plaintiffs’ attorney Niall McCarthy rejected that argument during trial. “They’re trying [to] blame the victim and say she shouldn’t have turned left in front of a car moving at that speed,” McCarthy said. The case also focused heavily on how much responsibility Morales’ parents bear for allowing their teenage son to drive. The plaintiffs argued there were warning signs surrounding Morales’ driving behavior and that his parents failed to adequately supervise him or intervene. Jurors heard evidence that Morales had previously been cited for driving more than 100 mph and for using his cell phone while driving. His parents testified they did not know about those specific citations. The defense disputed allegations about Morales’ parents owning the vehicle he was driving the night of the accident and presented vehicle registration and financial records as part of its argument. Jurors agreed on this point with the defense. “Parents are ultimately responsible for their teenage children,” Spiridon told NBC Bay Area before the verdict. “And based on the evidence, it appears to me the parents were not responsible for their teenage son.” The family’s attorney said following the verdict that he hoped the decision would serve as a warning to other parents. “We are hopeful today’s verdict serves as a wakeup call to Bay Area parents,” McCarthy said. “You cannot ignore warning signs with your teenage children.” The civil verdict follows years of separate criminal and juvenile court proceedings Because Morales was 17 at the time, his case proceeded in juvenile court. Prosecutors sought to have him transferred to adult court, but a judge denied that request. In 2024 a juvenile court judge found true two felony vehicular manslaughter allegations and felony allegations of engaging in a speed race causing great bodily injury. Morales served more than two years in juvenile hall followed by 90 days of electronic home monitoring and one year probation. The outcome frustrated members of the Ammen and Spiridon’s family. “It feels like Grace and Greg’s lives didn’t matter, that their daughter’s lives didn’t matter,” Liza Spiridon said. Harrison was prosecuted separately as an adult. He pleaded no contest to two counts of felony vehicular manslaughter and one count of felony street racing resulting in death or great bodily injury. In February 2025, a judge sentenced Harrison to eight years in state prison. Spiridon said Harrison apologized to the family during his sentencing and appeared deeply remorseful. “He was very remorseful, so much so that he turned around, even shackled to the chair, was crying and profusely apologizing,” Spiridon recalled. “Which meant a lot to our family.” But Harrison never made it to state prison on March 15, 2025, weeks after his sentencing, Harrison was found unresponsive at the Maple Street Correctional Center in Redwood City. The San Mateo County Coroner’s Office later determined Harrison died from the toxic effects of methadone, amitriptyline and gabapentin and ruled his death and accidental overdose from prescription drugs. Harrison’s death has since become the subject of a separate federal lawsuit. His parents and his estate are suing San Mateo County and others over his death in custody. The lawsuit alleges jail and medical personnel were responsible for medication-related failures that contributed to Harrison’s death. Those allegations have not been proven, and the county defendants have challenged the lawsuit. The case is still pending. Morales and his parents are also pursuing separate litigation against Redwood City, San Mateo County and other government entities over the investigation and prosecution following the crash. Their lawsuit alleges, among other claims, that authorities improperly characterized the collision as street racing and violated Morales’ constitutional rights. The government defendants have disputed the claims. The case was removed to federal court earlier this year, where the defendants filed motions seeking dismissal. Arnold Morales told NBC Bay Area during the trial that he would be willing to provide his family’s perspective after the verdict. NBC Bay Area reached out to him again following the jury’s decision and is awaiting a response.

headlines.title: FAA announces plans to partially roll back SFO restrictions, allow more landings
headlines.description: Restrictions placed on operating procedures at San Francisco International Airport will be revised by the Federal Aviation Administration on Wednesday, potentially increasing the number of aircraft that can be processed at one of the busiest airports in the country. Officials at the FAA and at SFO confirmed a previous ban on parallel approaches will be “slightly revised” to now included staggered arrivals, with the goal to maximize the use of the airport’s existing landing strips after losing the usage of others to planned maintenance. The new rules will allow, weather permitting, up to 42 aircrafts per hour, six more than before the change, but still less than what the airport maintained with parallel landings. It comes at a time when SFO is operating with reduced capacity because of ongoing maintenance to its runways, with one currently being used as a taxiway while the others alternating between landings and takeoffs. Doug Yakel, the airport’s spokesperson, confirmed the new staggered arrivals procedure is starting Wednesday. Airplanes will be arriving at staggered times, alternating which runway they use, which will help increase the number of landings and takeoffs in a limited timeframe. “While this will not fully restore the arrival rate we had when true side-by-side landings were permitted, this is nonetheless a step in the right direction,” said Yakel. SFO has two sets of parallel runways, with the center lines of each runway pair 750 feet from one another. According to the FAA, airports must ensure aircraft have a few thousand feet of horizontal separation for simultaneous operations. More steps are required depending on closeness, but no other airport in the U.S. shares the same frequency and distance of runways as SFO. Prior to March 30, SFO operated for decades under an FAA-approved waiver. The “double landings” saw aircraft land close to one another, with some passengers being able to see others on the adjacent plane. Pilots were instructed to carefully follow visual flight rules to maintain separation by watching neighboring airplanes and responding appropriately without air traffic control input. The practice became an iconic part of landing at SFO. United Airlines, who is the largest single carrier at SFO, praised the move to increase the number of aircraft movements. The Chicago-based airline said it “appreciated the FAA’s decision” and that the company had “been working closely with them to increase landing rates at SFO that safely make the best use of the airport’s capacity.” While the FAA has stated aircraft accidents did not prompt the banning of the parallel approaches, officials say safety is paramount at busy airports like SFO. While the airport is now allowed to clear up to 40 aircraft per hour for landings, it may increase to 42 by the end of the month. As of Wednesday afternoon, SFO remains capped at 36 arrivals an hour as a ground delay program is in place because of low visibility. Delays for flights from across the country and Canada are estimated to reach an hour.
headlines.source: Andres Jimenez Larios | Bay City News

headlines.title: Popular clothing store in San Jose's Japantown to close
headlines.description: Coldwater, the clothing store owned by three brothers in Japantown, is closing because the building was sold. Jason and his brothers Brian and Averill Nemedez are starting the painful transition of finding another place to operate Coldwater. The brothers each grew up with an interest in designing clothing, and developed individual lines they sold from their garage, ultimately leading to their own store. “Honestly, if you told me at 15 years old, we would be owning a shop in the heart of Japantown, I wouldn’t believe you. But we started doing this at a really young age, started doing art at a young age and just working and grinding, hustling got us to this point,” Jason Nemedez said. The name Coldwater pays homage to their grandmother and the street where the boys grew up. The Japantown shop attracted young buyers to, what they called, their ‘Jubo’ clothing line. Their designs are inspired by various influences including their Filipino culture. “It was easy. We just took a lot of pieces from our life, a lot of pieces from stories that we heard, we just translated it into art. We wanted to, basically, typically tell our story through art,” Jason said. Over four years, Coldwater evolved into a place for trendy and offbeat merchandise as well as a spot for community arts projects. But now the brothers say they need to find another space, because the building was sold. “It’s really disappointing. This place seems really unique. Especially because all of the neighbors seem really traditional. It’s a little more of a modern spot. I’m sad it’s closing,” San Jose resident Miya said. But the brothers have come too far to give up. “Yeah, very bittersweet. I’d like to see it more optimistically, taken that we’ve been here four years. We’ve, you know, contributed to the community around here, and try to enjoy the time we are here and looking forward to the opportunity in the future,” Brian said. “Heartbroken. But, you know, you can’t stay on that feeling for too long, you gotta keep moving, so we’re looking for new leads, so hopefully we’ll find a new spot and onto bigger and better things,” Jason said. Coldwater will be located on Fifth and Jackson Streets until Oct. 31, so while Japantown is celebrating Halloween, the brothers will be celebrating the end of this stage of their journey and moving on to the next.

headlines.title: Thousands of union workers in San Jose to vote on strike authorization
headlines.description: Thousands of workers from two of San Jose’s largest unions are voting this week on whether to authorize a strike. The International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers Local 21 and the Municipal Employees Federation, which together represent 4,500 city employees, have been in negotiations with the city for the past six months. Employees say the city’s latest offer of a 3% annual raise over three years doesn’t even keep up with inflation. “My rent is going up 8% next month, my daughter’s daycare just went up 6%,” Dylan Kuhlmann-Haley said. “The city’s last best final offer doesn’t meet that point. I’m going to be poorer tomorrow than I am today.” If the employees do strike, it could have major impacts on city services. Without enough staff, libraries may be forced to close and community centers may have to cancel after-school and senior programs. Striking workers would also include veterinarians and other staff at the city’s Animal Care Center and some employees at San Jose Mineta International Airport. Employees have until late Friday to vote on the strike authorization. The results will be announced Monday morning. In a statement, Mayor Matt Mahan said, “San Jose can’t spend money we don’t have…We found a way to offer modest raises because we believe we can support our workforce without compromising the most important services our residents depend on.” Employees say money isn’t the only sticking point. The unions are also asking the city to implement AI guardrails. “We just want to make sure that when it comes to contracting, when it comes to employees and what is expected of them, that there aren’t going to be layoffs and there aren’t going to be future reductions in staffing because of AI usage,” Michael Jun said.

headlines.title: Food pantry in Hayward to close after more than 50 years of service
headlines.description: A food pantry in Hayward that’s been serving the community for over 50 years will shut down at the end of the week. South Hayward Parish’s last day of food distribution will be Friday, First Presbyterian Church of Hayward announced. The site’s emergency shelter and resource center for unhoused residents will stay open. “We have worked and prayed to discern how to best steward our resources and live our mission to meet community needs, and it has become clear that operating both a food pantry and shelter on the same campus is no longer sustainable,” FirstPres Hayward said in a statement on its website. “Therefore, we have made the difficult decision to discontinue food pantry operations so we can focus fully on serving our unhoused neighbors.” The emergency shelter provides year-round access for 25 unhoused residents, and the daytime resource centers offers case management, meals, showers, laundry, and housing and healthcare connections, according to FirstPres Hayward. “While the number of individuals we house can’t increase because of space restrictions, the programs we provide can become more robust, ensuring more guests are connected to housing more quickly, and therefore making a greater impact on the experience of homelessness in South Hayward,” FirstPres Hayward said in a statement. Alternative food distribution sites in the area can be found below.

headlines.title: 1 dead, 1 hurt in Richmond stabbing
headlines.description: One person died and another was injured in a stabbing in Richmond, police said Wednesday. Richmond police said they received a report at about 11:18 p.m. Tuesday of a stabbing in the 1700 block of Wood Place. Responding officers and medical personnel found two victims suffering from stab wounds, according to police. Both victims were transported to the hospital to be treated, but one victim did not survive. The other victim was listed in stable condition and is expected to survive. Homicide unit detectives responded to the stabbing scene and took over the investigation. Police did not immediately release any information about a suspect. Investigators believe the stabbing was an isolated incident, police said, adding that there was no active threat to the community. An investigation is underway. Anyone with information is asked to call the Richmond Police Department at 510-233-1214.
